heading: Messy neurons come from architecture, regularization and weak tools, not capacity
definition: messy late-layer neurons come from architecture, regularization and weak tools, so the share of interpretable neurons rises with better tools and modern architectures (the essay's estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models go from about 5% to about 99%).
summary: Independent groups show that architecture, regularization and interpretation tools change how interpretable units are in vision CNNs, GANs, toy models and small language models, though some newer designs lower interpretability rather than raise it. Several studies also find that layer width matters, against the 'not capacity' part, and no other study measures the essay's estimated rise in interpretable neurons from about 5% to about 99%.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: R2 that training choices, not just width, set neuron monosemanticity (2211.09169 and 2312.03096, different groups), with width and feature-density effects also shown. <1B (vision CNNs, GANs, small LMs; most vision models fall under counts V4.studies_by_size 'not stated'): R2 that architecture, regularization and readout tools change unit interpretability, with mixed direction. 1-10B and 10-100B: R0 by independent work, from one non-original study (2604.02178, MoE routing, probe proxy). >100B: untested (counts V4.studies_by_size has no >100B key). The essay's numeric InceptionV1/ConvNeXt estimates (about 5% to about 99%): R0, author estimates that no other study measures.
suggested_status.reason: Counts: V4.studies_tested 17. V4.verdicts: supports in 12 studies, limits_scope in 13, challenges in 2. V4.tested_sharing_an_author_with_an_original 0. V4.tested_by_review_class: reviewed 8, preprint 6. V4.tested_with_controls 15. V4.rows_by_state: observed 54, partial 32, absent 17, reversed 26, cannot_determine 19. Groups other than the essay's show that architecture, regularization and readout tools change unit interpretability: vision CNNs (1711.05611, 2501.05398), GANs (1811.10597), toys (2211.09169), and LMs (2604.02178, 2611.03655, 2503.07639, 2607.08946). These are mostly controlled retraining comparisons. The direction is not uniform. Newer architectures lower or leave it unchanged in ViT (2501.05398), GEGLU/SoLU/fine-grained MoE (2503.07639), standard MoE (2611.03655) and LWTA DeiT-T (2310.04929). The 'not capacity' clause is challenged: 2501.05398 attributes narrow ResNet18's polysemanticity to a too-small basis, and 1711.05611, 2211.09169 and 2503.07639 report width effects. 2410.16443 challenges the claim at one layer. No study measures the InceptionV1 or ConvNeXt shares. So R2 holds for 'architecture, regularization and tools matter', not for 'not capacity' or the numeric estimates.
suggested_status.open_questions: Several results would change this. (1) A share measurement, with one tool and one threshold, of InceptionV1 vs same-size ConvNeXt late-layer neurons, read with era and modern tools; this tests the numeric part. (2) A width sweep at a fixed architecture and tool in a modern LM; this would settle 'not capacity'. (3) Matched GELU vs SwiGLU dense LMs scored on a common neuron metric. (4) Standard MoE vs dense on one shared metric, to resolve the conflict between 2611.03655 and 2604.02178/2503.07639. (5) Any test above 100B or on post-trained models.

original_result.setup: The author re-read InceptionV1's last layer with better visualization tools, retrained it with modern regularization, compared a ConvNeXt of the same size, and shrank layers to see how less capacity affects their neurons.
original_result.result: By the author's own estimates, the share of interpretable last-layer neurons rises from about 5% with the tools of the time to about 50% with better tools, about 70% after retraining with modern regularization, and about 99% in the ConvNeXt. When InceptionV1 layer 3b was cut from 480 to 10 neurons, or a ConvNeXt final layer from 1,024 to 13, the neurons stayed interpretable but coarser (covering broader patterns) rather than becoming mixtures, and a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on the shrunken layer did not recover clean curve-detector neurons.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Deeper CNN architectures had more unique concept detectors in the last conv layer.
GAN architecture tweaks that improved quality raised interpretable units and concept types.
Progressive GAN architecture variants raised concept diversity and semantic-matching units.
Deeper, more modern CNNs yielded more unique detectors; batch norm lowered interpretability.
Toy models with equal loss ranged from mostly polysemantic to mostly monosemantic, depending on training choices.
Polysemantic neurons appeared in a toy autoencoder even with more neurons than features.
On one probe dataset, LWTA (winner-take-all) DeiT-S topped a published ResNet-50's labelled-neuron share by 9–10 points.
L1 activation-sparsity training made neurons' concepts clearer in all four vision models trained on ImageNet subsets.
Mixture-of-experts layers (Switch, MoE-X) beat dense GELU layers on chess-model interpretability at equal active parameters.
OLMoE-1B-7B was cleaner than OLMo-7B, and cleanliness rose with sparser routing.
In a legibility-focused transformer, a tuned lens (learned readout) raised nameable-output units from 38.7% to 65.3%.
At equal active compute, MoWE (mixture-of-experts variant) had coordinates judged more concept-specific than a dense model's.
Adding batch normalization significantly lowered Places205-AlexNet interpretability at equal accuracy.
As a share of units, VGG, not ResNet, had the most unique concept detectors.
Monosemanticity rose with width and nearly vanished when features were dense (often active), regardless of training.
In a toy autoencoder, polysemanticity arising by chance persisted until neuron count neared feature count squared.
At matched size, LWTA (winner-take-all) layers in DeiT-T did not raise the share of labelled neurons.
Only about 0.7–26% of final-layer ResNet-50 features qualified for individual explanation with a CLIP-based tool.
CRATE, a white-box transformer, scored higher than GPT-2 on neuron interpretability, but scores stayed about 5–11%.
A pre-trained ViT had less clear, more polysemantic neurons than the ResNets; gains from sparsity varied.
Other activation functions and fine-grained mixture-of-experts layers scored below dense GELU layers on chess-model interpretability.
Even a tuned lens left about 35% of units unnameable; final-layer nameability stayed near 10%.
A standard mixture-of-experts model scored below the dense model, no better than a randomly rotated basis.
CLIP ViT-L MLP neurons all appeared polysemantic, each mixing 3–4 unrelated features.

sources.source_id: TITLE:Language models can explain neurons in language models
sources.headline: Sparser activations raised scores for LLM-written neuron explanations but cost parameter efficiency; scores stayed low overall.
One-layer CRATE (a white-box transformer) scored below a one-layer GPT on all three neuron interpretability metrics.
Narrow ResNet18 was more polysemantic than wider ResNets; the authors attribute this to capacity.

counting_note: Each group counts distinct sources for this claim. The same source can appear in more than one group or claim; counts are not votes.

untested.what: The essay's numeric share estimates. InceptionV1's last layer at about 5% with era tools, about 50% with better tools, about 70% retrained with modern regularization, and a same-size ConvNeXt at about 99%. No non-original study states a numeric share for InceptionV1 or ConvNeXt. GoogLeNet (InceptionV1) appears only in Network Dissection. It is in the unique-detector count ranking (1704.05796#r6; 1711.05611#r2, #r7) and in 1711.05611's figures. Those figures also plot its ratio of unique detectors per unit (Fig. 9; layer-wise on Places365 in Fig. 13), which is share-like but figure-only. They also show detector examples (Fig. 11) and unique object detectors vs accuracy (Fig. 26). The text states no numeric share or ratio for GoogLeNet. No non-original study includes a ConvNeXt.
untested.basis: The 'untested parts of V4' lines of nearly every study name the 5%→99% / InceptionV1 estimates: 1704.05796, 1711.05611, 2310.04929, 2312.03096, 2501.05398, 2604.02178, 2611.03655, 2307.10504, lw:bCtbuWraqYTDtuARg, 1811.10597, 1901.09887, 2211.09169, 2503.07639, 2607.08946, 2410.16443, and the OpenAI paper. Counts: V4.studies_with_untested_parts is 16. The essay's R12 is marked cannot_determine, 'a recollection, not a measurement'. The check of 1711.05611 finds GoogLeNet's per-unit ratio only in Figs. 9 and 13, with no number in the text.

untested.what: An old vs new reading tool on the same vision classifier's late-layer neurons, measured as a share. Tool comparisons exist only for a GAN generator (segmentation vs human labels) and a purpose-built 125M LM (raw vs tuned lens). FALCON applies one tool. Network Dissection's human-vs-dissection comparison is not in rows.
untested.basis: Untested lines: 1704.05796 and 1711.05611 ('Whether better explanation tools raise the interpretable share'), 2310.04929 ('Effect of better tools on the share'), 2501.05398 ('No test that better explanation tools raise the interpretable share'). Not-in-rows line of 1711.05611 (Table 3).

untested.what: Conventional regularization (such as weight decay or dropout) as a cause of messy neurons in standard language models. Effects of such regularizers on unit interpretability are measured only in vision CNNs (SemanticLens, Network Dissection) and toy networks. One LM study varies purpose-built legibility penalties instead, on bounded operands. In 2607.08946's 125M bounded-unit LM (single seed), raising the between-unit decorrelation weight λd from 0 to 1 in otherwise unchanged training moves Selective% from 78.7 to 62.2 (non-monotone). The same change shrinks a concept's co-firing group from a median 562 units to a single unit. A variance floor on top of the crispness penalty raises the FFN selective share from 2% to 25%. 2611.03655 varies router regularization only in a toy appendix (A.2), scored by routing mutual information, and in an LM router screen scored by loss, not readability. 2604.02178 and the OpenAI paper do not isolate regularization.
untested.basis: Untested lines of 2604.02178 ('roles of regularization and tool quality are not isolated'), 2611.03655 ('Regularization and capacity not isolated'), 2607.08946 ('Regularization effects are measured only…'), and the OpenAI paper ('Neither is regularization…'). The 2607.08946 line holds only for conventional regularizers: the check of that study finds decorrelation, crispness and variance-floor penalties swept in its LM training. The check of 2611.03655 places router regularization only in toy appendix A.2 and the LM router screen.

wording_issues.phrase: rises with better tools and modern architectures
wording_issues.issue: Newer architectures go both ways. Raises: ResNet/DenseNet over older CNNs by count (1711.05611#r5), MoE routing in pretrained LMs (2604.02178#r7), MoWE (0.523 vs Dense 0.375, 2611.03655#r5), Switch/MoE-X on chess. Lowers or leaves unchanged: ViT vs ResNet (2501.05398#r1, #r2), CLIP ViT-L neurons all polysemantic, matched DeiT-T LWTA (negligible or 1.4–2.2 point drops), GEGLU 0.255 and SoLU 0.306 vs GELU 0.356 coverage, Standard MoE 0.268 vs Dense 0.375, BatchNorm. 'Modern' doesn't predict the direction in these results.

Width and size effects are reported in several settings. Narrow ResNet18 is more polysemantic, attributed by its authors to a too-small basis (challenges verdict). AlexNet conv5 unique detectors rise when width triples, then plateau at 1024/2048 units. Toy monosemantic count rises with width, and dense features force polysemanticity. Chess coverage rises with MLP width (0.53 at α=16) and model size. In about 3M LMs, the interpretability gain from sparse activations costs parameter efficiency: density 0.01 is about 40% less efficient (OpenAI, from text).

wording_issues.phrase: messy late-layer neurons come from architecture, regularization
wording_issues.issue: The direction depends on which regularizer is used. L1 activation sparsity raises clarity (ResNet34 45.0% to 60.2%). Dropout raises VGG clarity (41.8% to 47.1%). Batch normalization lowers interpretability at equal accuracy. Removing dropout shifts detector types (more textures, fewer objects). In a toy autoencoder, l1 regularization comes with incidental polysemanticity. Negative bias and bias weight decay produce monosemantic neurons. The same BatchNorm result is filed as supports by the 1711.05611 verdict (regularization causing messiness) and as limits_scope by the 1704.05796 verdict (a modern component lowering interpretability).

These tests measure something other than a share: unique-detector counts (Network Dissection), mean simulation scores with no threshold (CRATE), k=1 probe F1 (2604.02178), judge-scored coordinate specificity (MoWE), chess BSP coverage (MoE-X), embedding-based clarity and polysemanticity (SemanticLens), and classification-layer exact-label accuracy (DISCOVER). Network Dissection's per-unit ratio of unique detectors ranks VGG, not ResNet, highest (figure-only). Share-like numbers appear in 2607.08946 (FFN operands decodable to a nameable category, whole model: 38.7% through the raw logit lens, 65.3% in the raw or the unit's own tuned frame), 2307.10504 (supervised ResNet-50: 0.68% of final-layer features qualify), 1811.10597 (154 of 201 human-consistent units labelled, a count), 2211.09169 (toy decoders with negative-bias training: 30–50% of neurons monosemantic) and 1711.05611 Table 3 (from text, not in rows). That table gives human-rated interpretable units per AlexNet layer, with human descriptions from earlier work as the baseline, as units out of layer width: conv1 57/96, conv2 126/256, conv3 247/384, conv4 258/384, conv5 194/256.

wording_issues.phrase: messy late-layer neurons come from ... weak tools
wording_issues.issue: In the legible transformer (125M, single seed), final-layer decodability is about 10%, and the tuned lens is near identity there. The authors say that residue is genuine, not a tool artifact. The text gives no separate raw and tuned final-layer numbers. About 35% of units stay undecodable in both the raw frame and their own tuned frame (verdict reason; 65.3% decode in either frame, whole model). FALCON finds that most final-layer ResNet-50 features don't qualify for individual explanation (supervised 0.68%).

wording_issues.phrase: the essay's estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models go from about 5% to about 99%
wording_issues.issue: These are the author's own estimates, not measurements. R12 (about 5%) is a recollection, marked cannot_determine. R13–R15 (about 50%, about 70%, about 99%) are labelled estimates. The R15 note says the intro gives '99-100%'. No study in the pack measures a share on InceptionV1 or ConvNeXt.

Several supporting results score units that are not hidden neurons. MoWE scores FFN-update output coordinates; its verdict says 'Unit is output coordinates, not hidden neurons'. 2604.02178 scores best-layer, best-expert probes over expert neurons. 2607.08946 scores decoded unit writes in a purpose-built bounded-unit model. MoE-X's language results use an automated scorer, but its chess metrics measure alignment with board properties.

method_sensitivity.factor: Measure: count vs share; metric variant; depth
method_sensitivity.what: Network Dissection ranks ResNet highest by unique-detector count but VGG highest by per-unit ratio (from text). CRATE vs GPT reverses with depth: at 1 layer CRATE is lower on all three metrics (top-and-random 3.9 vs 8.8). At 2 layers it is higher (top-and-random 8.05 vs 4.2; Anthropic 11.35 vs 10.2, a small gain).

DeiT-S LWTA vs cited ResNet-50: CIFAR-100 Train 46.20% to 55.20%, but Broden 70.50% to 68.30%. In matched DeiT-T, results range from a 1-point gain (ImageNet Val, 95.00% to 96.00%) to a 2.2-point drop (CIFAR-100 Train, 53.00% to 50.80%). Network Dissection's problems line notes that concepts missing from Broden may not score.

Legible 125M model (annealed, single seed), whole model: 38.7% of feed-forward unit writes (7131 of 18432) decode to a nameable content category through the raw logit lens. Read in either frame (raw or the unit's own tuned lens), 65.3% do. The 65.3% is not a tuned-lens-only figure; the text notes the tuned lens can hurt units that were already canonical. The gain sits mid-stack (one layer 15% to 73%). The final layer stays at about 10%, with the lens near identity there; the authors call this genuine, not a rotation. The text gives no separate raw and tuned final-layer numbers. Segmentation dissection vs human labels: 154 of 201 human-consistent GAN units recovered (a count). OpenAI: scores rise with explainer capability and revision (from text).

method_sensitivity.what: FALCON's high-activation threshold α is chosen per representation space, so its explainable share (supervised ResNet-50 0.68%, aggregate roughly 20%) is a threshold-dependent upper bound. Network Dissection, AlexNet conv5 on Places205 with activation threshold τ from 0.0025 to 0.04: a larger τ, or no threshold, gives more color, texture and large-region labels, and τ below 0.005 finds fewer objects (Discussion, Fig. 28; not in rows). The 'relative orderings remain stable' statement is about the IoU detector threshold, not τ: different IoU thresholds change detector counts but keep orderings (Sec. 2.2). The essay's method line says its percentages depend on where the 'one thing' threshold is set.

method_sensitivity.factor: Basis: native vs randomly rotated coordinates
method_sensitivity.what: Dense native and rotated coordinate specificity are equal (0.375 and 0.375). Standard MoE native 0.268 vs rotated 0.289; the verdict gives the difference's CI as including zero. MoWE native 0.523 vs rotated 0.384. Whether 'architecture helps' depends on testing against the rotation control.

method_sensitivity.factor: Routing sparsity, probe k and layer selection
method_sensitivity.what: Expert-level cleanliness rises as the active-to-total ratio NA/N falls. The sparsest model is Qwen3-30B-A3B (NA/N≈0.06). Mixtral-8x7B (NA/N=0.25) is noticeably lower. The MoE–dense gap is largest at k=1. Best-layer selection is an upper-bound strategy.

The same L1 setting (λ=80) cuts polysemanticity in ResNet34 (91.5% to 67.0%) but barely moves it in ResNet50 (89.3% to 87.7%) or VGG-13 (83.3% to 83.2%). Dropout changes VGG models, while ResNets are essentially unaffected (verdict citing Table G.1).

method_sensitivity.factor: Training recipe and hidden size in toys
method_sensitivity.what: At equal loss, learning rate, negative initial bias and bias weight decay move toy decoders from mostly polysemantic to mostly monosemantic (503 of 512 features with one monosemantic neuron; 30–50% of neurons monosemantic). On the absolute-value task, a negative initial bias is not enough on its own: either slower weight decay or a high learning rate is also needed (Sec 4, Sec 4.3, Figs 22–23). In the l1 autoencoder, the polysemantic count scales as Θ(n²/m) with hidden size m.
